lesson.title: Who Do You Think You Are? Building the Self-Concept
lesson.summary: Self-concept is the organized set of beliefs a person holds about who they are, and Carl Rogers argued that psychological health depends on how well this self-image matches a person's actual, lived experience.
lesson.body:
Self-concept is simply the answer, or the whole collection of answers, a person gives to the question "who am I?" It includes beliefs about one's own traits, abilities, values, roles, and history, all organized into a more or less coherent picture of the self. Everyone has one, but Rogers, building on the broader humanistic framework introduced in the previous chapter, treated the self-concept as central to understanding personality and psychological health.

Rogers used a specific pair of terms to describe how self-concept can go right or wrong. He distinguished between a person's real self, roughly, their self-concept as it actually stands right now, and their ideal self, who they feel they ought to be or wish they were. When these two are reasonably close, Rogers called the state congruence, and associated it with good psychological adjustment. When there is a large gap between them, or more broadly when a person's self-concept does not match their actual felt experience, Rogers called that incongruence, and linked it to anxiety and psychological distress.

This connects directly back to unconditional positive regard. A child raised under conditional regard learns to filter out or deny feelings and experiences that clash with the conditions of worth they picked up from caregivers, keeping only the parts of themselves that reliably earned approval. Over time that filtering process can leave someone with a self-concept that no longer matches their genuine, full experience, which is exactly the incongruence Rogers considered a root of psychological difficulty.

Self-concept is also shaped by the explanations people give for their own outcomes, which is where attribution theory comes in. If a student attributes a good grade on a test to their own ability and effort, "I'm capable, and I worked hard for this," that attribution feeds directly into a self-concept as a competent student. If instead the student attributes the same grade to luck or an easy test, it barely touches their self-image at all. Two students can even receive the exact same grade, a B, and build very different self-concepts out of it: one absorbs it as evidence of being a generally capable student having an ordinary off day, while the other absorbs it as proof that they simply are not smart. The outcome was identical, but the pattern of self-relevant attributions each student made turned that same raw experience into two very different building blocks for who they believe themselves to be.
